title: Wat Buppharam, Trat — Trat's Oldest Temple, 370 Years Old | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A guide to Wat Buppharam (Wat Plai Khlong), Trat's oldest temple, built in the reign of King Prasat Thong. See the old wooden viharn, mural paintings and the temple's artefact museum, plus how to get there, opening hours and what not to miss.
keywords: Wat Buppharam Trat, Wat Plai Khlong, oldest temple in Trat, Wat Buppharam museum, things to do in Trat
intro: Wat Buppharam — known to locals by its old name, Wat Plai Khlong — is the oldest temple in Trat province. It was built back in the Ayutthaya period, in the reign of King Prasat Thong, which puts it well past 370 years old. You'll find an old wooden viharn here, mural paintings, a row of stupas along the canal, and a museum of artefacts the temple has collected itself. If you're into history and traditional craftsmanship, it's worth a stop.

blocks.html: If you're visiting Trat and want to see more than just the sea and the islands, Wat Buppharam is a good place to stop. The temple sits about 2 kilometres west of Trat town, in Ban Plai Khlong, Wang Krachae subdistrict — which is why locals call it Wat Plai Khlong. It's shaded by big old trees, with a small canal running through, and the atmosphere is quiet — none of the crowds you get at the famous temples in bigger cities. An easy place to wander around.

blocks.text: A short history — just how old?

blocks.html: According to the temple's own records, Buppharam was built around 1652, in the reign of King Prasat Thong of Ayutthaya. That makes it roughly 370-something years old today — the oldest temple in Trat province. The name "Buppharam" means "the monastery of flowers," and it comes from a story: when the local landowner and villagers set out to find a place to build a temple, they reached this spot and caught the scent of fragrant flowers drifting in the air — but could never find the tree it came from. They took it as a good omen and built the temple right here.

In 2001, Wat Buppharam received an award for outstanding architectural conservation from the Association of Siamese Architects (ASA) — confirmation that the old craftsmanship here is genuinely valued and has been well looked after.

items.label: Day trips from Trat
items.note: Out and back in a day

items: The old wooden viharn — the timber building the temple is known for. The structure and the wooden ceiling are still largely in their original state, and it's a favourite spot for anyone who loves wooden architecture to stop and take photos.
The murals in the ordination hall — inside the ubosot are old paintings that blend Ayutthaya and Chinese styles, with details that really capture the era.
The stupas along the canal — several old stupas line the canal, with weathered laterite walls and frangipani trees growing in among them. The atmosphere is very classic.
The Buddha's Footprint mondop — a building enshrining a replica of the Buddha's footprint, another spot where people come to pay their respects.
Luang Pho To — the large principal Buddha image that Trat locals hold in high regard, and a regular stop for prayers and blessings.

blocks.html: What sets this temple apart from the rest is the museum the temple set up to house the artefacts it has collected over the years. Inside you'll find Buddha images in various postures, old crockery and ceramic ware, antique pottery from both Sukhothai and China, ancient palm-leaf manuscripts, a busabok throne, plus brassware and any number of other art objects. It's like a miniature treasury of old Trat that's genuinely enjoyable to browse.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: The museum is open daily, roughly 8:00–17:00. There's no official entry fee, but there's a donation box if you'd like to chip in toward the temple's upkeep. If you want to see the woodwork and the paintings clearly, go mid-morning before the sun gets harsh — the light inside the viharn is soft and just right.

items.name: Trat Old Town (Bang Phra canalside community)
items.blurb: An old community along Bang Phra canal, with wooden houses, coffee shops and local eats. It's in the town centre, just a few minutes' drive from the temple.

items.name: Markets in Trat town
items.blurb: Local food, shrimp paste, dried seafood and Trat souvenirs — a good stop after the temple.

blocks.text: Getting there and the best time to go

items: From Trat town — drive about 2 kilometres west toward Ban Plai Khlong, Wang Krachae subdistrict. There are signs pointing the way in, and both cars and motorbikes can reach the temple entrance.
Parking — there's a parking area inside the temple grounds, big enough that you won't need to worry about finding a spot.
When to go — it's fine any time of day, but morning through late morning is shadier and best for photos. Avoid midday when the sun is strong.
What to wear — this is a temple and a sacred place, so dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, especially when entering the ordination hall and the museum.

blocks.html: You can see all of Wat Buppharam in about 45 minutes to an hour. It works well as the opening or closing stop on your first day in Trat, before or after you catch a boat out to the islands — a chance to see another side of the province beyond the sea.

faq.q: How old is Wat Buppharam in Trat?
faq.a: Wat Buppharam was built around 1652, in the reign of King Prasat Thong during the Ayutthaya period, making it roughly 370-something years old — the oldest temple in Trat province. Older locals still call it by another name, Wat Plai Khlong, after where it stands.

faq.q: What are the museum's hours at Wat Buppharam, and is there an entry fee?
faq.a: The museum is open daily, roughly 8:00–17:00. There's no official entry fee — just a donation box if you'd like to contribute toward the temple's upkeep. Inside it displays Buddha images, antique pottery, palm-leaf manuscripts and many other artefacts.

faq.q: Is Wat Buppharam far from Trat town?
faq.a: Not far — it's about 2 kilometres west of Trat town, in Ban Plai Khlong, Wang Krachae subdistrict. It's only a few minutes' drive, and there's parking inside the temple grounds.

faq.q: What's worth seeing at Wat Buppharam?
faq.a: The highlights are the old wooden viharn, the murals in the ordination hall that blend Ayutthaya and Chinese styles, the old stupas along the canal, the Buddha's Footprint mondop, Luang Pho To, and the temple's museum of artefacts.

faq.q: How should I dress to visit Wat Buppharam?
faq.a: It's a temple and a sacred place, so dress modestly with shoulders and knees covered, especially when entering the ordination hall and the museum. Remove your shoes before going into the buildings, as the signs indicate.
